title: A filter at every door
hook: Most families in India have never used your machine. How will you get them to buy it?

future.label: Trust
future.hint: How many homes know your name and keep coming back

intro.text: Bombay, 1982. The Tata group's Forbes company and Sweden's Electrolux start a company together, and you run it. Your first product is the Euroclean vacuum cleaner, but most Indian homes have never seen one and still sweep with a broom. You must find buyers before your money runs out.

d1.title: Where should you sell?
d1.setup: Shops already sell fans and radios across India. Dealers can reach many towns. But most people have never seen your machine work. Your team is small, and you have little money.
d1.question: Where will you sell your first machine?
d1.advisor: Shops can reach many buyers without us hiring more people. But someone may need to show families how the machine works.

options.label: Use appliance shops. Dealers pay for space and stock, but may not explain the machine.
options.outcome: Dealers put your machine beside the fans. Shoppers look at it, but few know why they need it. Dealers spend little time explaining it, so most boxes stay on the shelf for months.
options.why: People do not know why they need this new machine. No one asks how they clean today or what dust costs them before showing the machine. Remember: ask what the problem costs them before you show the fix.
options.better: Send salespeople to homes. First ask families what dust and sweeping cost them. Then show the machine working.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you sold a new machine through shops. More people may buy after seeing it work.

options.label: Visit homes and show the machine. Each family gets a demo, but visits cost time and money.
options.outcome: You open no shops. Your salespeople carry the machine into homes and show how it works. This takes time and hard work. By 1987, you still have just one office in Bombay and 20 salespeople. The company is struggling.
options.why: Families need to see how this new machine works. At home, your salesperson can ask how much time and work dust costs them. Then they can show the machine. Remember: ask what the problem costs them before you show the fix.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you took your machine into homes. Families could see how it helped them.

options.label: Open large city showrooms. Buyers can see demos, but you pay rent while waiting.
options.outcome: Visitors like the demo, but few people come. Most families will not travel to see a machine they do not think they need. You keep paying rent while the machines wait.
options.why: Showing the machine helped, but few buyers came. No one visited their homes to ask what sweeping cost them. Remember: ask what the problem costs them before you show the fix.
options.better: Take the machine into homes. Ask families what dust and sweeping cost them. Then show it working on their own floor.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you waited for buyers to visit your showrooms. You needed to reach more families.

text.text: It is the late 1980s. Your vacuum cleaners are still in shops, but sales are low. You add Aquaguard, a water purifier for the kitchen. This time, you send salespeople into homes.
It is the late 1980s. Few people visit your showrooms. You add Aquaguard, a water purifier for the kitchen. You also start sending salespeople into homes.
It is the late 1980s. Your salespeople now carry another machine into homes: Aquaguard, a water purifier for the kitchen. Few Indian homes have used one before.

d2.title: Why pay when boiling is cheap?
d2.setup: Families keep telling your salespeople the same thing. Boiling water costs almost nothing. Your purifier costs a lot for most families, and your salespeople hear "no" again and again.
d2.question: How will you answer families who say your purifier costs too much?
d2.advisor: Families think boiling costs nothing. We could make our price easier to pay, but they may still ask why they need the machine.

options.label: Keep the price and explain boiling costs. Each visit takes longer, but families see the full cost.
options.outcome: You keep the price and explain the costs of boiling water to each family. Visits take longer, but more families buy Aquaguard each year instead of boiling their tap water.
options.why: Families compared your price with boiling because they thought boiling was free. But boiling uses fuel and time every day. Illness can cost much more. You changed what they compared your price with. Remember: when they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"
options.takeaway: In the 1980s you kept your price and showed families what boiling water really costs.

options.label: Keep the price and offer monthly payments. More may sign up, but collecting money takes work.
options.outcome: More families agree to buy because the monthly payment looks small. But many still wonder why they should pay when boiling works. Some stop paying before the full amount is paid. Your team spends time asking for the money.
options.why: Monthly payments help families who already want the machine. But many still think boiling costs nothing, so they do not see why they should pay. Remember: when they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"
options.better: Keep the price. Show families what boiling costs in fuel, time and doctor's bills. This helps them see why the purifier costs more.
options.takeaway: In the 1980s you made payments smaller, but families still did not see why the machine was worth buying.

options.label: Cut the price by a third. More families may buy, but you earn less on each sale.
options.outcome: More families buy, but each sale now barely pays for your salesperson. Many still compare your machine with boiling, which they think is free. Some also wonder why you cut the price.
options.why: Even after the price cut, your machine costs more than boiling seems to cost. You also earn less on each sale. Families still need to understand what boiling really costs. Remember: when they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"
options.better: Keep the price. Show families what boiling costs in fuel, time and doctor's bills. This helps them see why the purifier costs more.
options.takeaway: In the 1980s you cut your price, but families still thought boiling cost nothing.

d3.title: After the sale

setup.text: It is the 1990s. Thousands of homes own your purifier, but your price cut means you earn little on each sale. Every machine needs to be fitted to a tap, and its filter wears out. Your salespeople earn most of their pay from new sales, so they want to find new buyers.

It is the 1990s. Thousands of homes own your purifier, but your team spends hours collecting monthly payments. Every machine needs to be fitted to a tap, and its filter wears out. Your salespeople earn most of their pay from new sales, so they want to find new buyers.

It is the 1990s. Thousands of homes own your purifier. Every machine needs to be fitted to a tap, and its filter wears out. Your salespeople earn most of their pay from new sales, so they want to find new buyers.

d3.question: How will you care for machines after selling them?
d3.advisor: Our salespeople earn money from new buyers. But old customers also need help, and that takes time away from selling.

options.label: Use local mechanics for service. Salespeople can find new buyers, but you control repairs less.
options.outcome: Sales continue, but local mechanics fit some machines badly and use cheap filters. When the water tastes strange, families blame your company and tell their neighbours. Some go back to boiling water.
options.why: A sale is not the end. Families who trust your service may buy more filters, repairs and another machine from you. All these buys add to customer lifetime value. Remember: a customer is worth the margin on all their future buys.
options.better: Fit the machines with your own staff. Send technicians back often and offer yearly service plans.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you left repairs to local mechanics. Poor service made families trust you less.

options.label: Repair machines when owners call. You earn a fee for each visit, but problems may go unnoticed.
options.outcome: You earn a little money from each repair visit. But most owners call only after a machine stops working. Some have already gone back to boiling water. Few buy another machine from you.
options.why: When you wait for a call, you only visit after something goes wrong. Some families stop using the machine and stop buying from you. Regular visits can also help you get another order. Remember: a customer is worth the margin on all their future buys.
options.better: Fit the machines with your own staff. Send technicians back often and offer yearly service plans.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you waited for repair calls. More families might have stayed if you had visited them regularly.

options.label: Use your own staff for fitting and service. Families get regular care, but you need more workers.
options.outcome: Your company's plumbers fit the purifiers, and your technicians return to service them. You open labs to test water and sell yearly service plans. Families who trust your service keep buying filters and plans from you, year after year.
options.why: One machine can bring years of income through filters, plans and future machines. This is customer lifetime value. Each visit can also help you get another order. Remember: a customer is worth the margin on all their future buys.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you kept caring for the machines you sold. Families trusted you and kept buying.

text.text: It is 2005. You now have thousands of young salespeople. Most earn money from each sale. Your earlier price cut means they earn less per sale, and many towns know your company for badly fitted machines. Good sellers leave, and it gets harder to sell.
It is 2005. You now have thousands of young salespeople. Most earn money from each sale. Your earlier price cut means they earn less per sale, so many good sellers leave.

It is 2005. You now have thousands of young salespeople. Most earn money from each sale. But badly fitted machines have hurt your name in many towns. More families now refuse to let your salespeople in.

It is 2005. Three of every four water purifiers sold in India are yours. You have about 5,300 young salespeople, aged 26 on average. Most earn money from each sale. But training, offices and motorbikes cost you money every month.

It is 2005. You have about 5,300 young salespeople, aged 26 on average. Each gets three weeks of training to show the machine and make a sale. Most earn money from each sale. But training, offices and motorbikes cost you money every month.

d4.title: How much does each sale cost?

setup.text: It is 2012. You have close to 9 million customer homes, but your share of purifier sales has fallen from three in four to about six in ten. Rivals sell in shops. More people live in gated buildings, where visiting homes is harder. About 7,500 of your people still visit homes to sell.

It is 2012. Rivals sell purifiers in shops, and your share of sales is falling. More families now live in gated buildings, where visiting homes is harder. Your large home sales team costs more each year.

d4.question: How will you sell purifiers as home visits become harder and more costly?
d4.advisor: Our home sales team costs more each year. But families know our name because our people visited them.

options.label: Hire thousands more sellers. You can visit more homes, but your pay bill will rise.
options.outcome: Your pay bill rises sharply, but guards stop many new salespeople at the gate. Each extra sale costs more than the one before. You keep earning less from each new sale.
options.why: More visits only help when a sale earns more than it costs to get that buyer. Gated buildings made each extra sale cost more. Remember: each customer must earn more margin than winning them cost.
options.better: Check the cost of getting a buyer through each way of selling. Keep home demos where they pay, and sell simpler models in shops.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you hired more sellers without checking the cost of each sale. Your earnings from each sale kept falling.

options.label: Sell basic models in shops and costly ones through home demos. You may lose some sellers.
options.outcome: You find that home visits earn enough for costly machines, but not for basic ones. You sell basic models in shops and keep home demos for costly ones. Your sales team gets smaller, and some loyal sellers leave angry. But each sale costs you less.
options.why: Home visits helped you grow, but they do not always pay for themselves now. You compared what each sale cost with what it earned. This is LTV:CAC. Remember: each customer must earn more margin than winning them cost.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you checked what each sale cost and changed how you sold, even though some sellers left.

options.label: Keep home sales and use online ads for demos. Buyers can request visits, but each visit still costs money.
options.outcome: You keep your sales team because it is a big part of your company. Online ads bring requests for home demos. In 2014, you still have more than 8,000 salespeople, while rivals continue selling in shops.
options.why: Families who ask for a demo are easier to sell to, so online ads helped. But every sale still needed a paid home visit. You also missed buyers who shop in stores. Remember: each customer must earn more margin than winning them cost.
options.better: Check the cost of getting a buyer through each way of selling. Keep home demos where they pay, and sell simpler models in shops.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you kept home sales as your main way to sell. You still needed to check the cost of each sale.

legend.title: A name families trust
legend.text: You keep home visits for costly machines and sell simpler ones in shops. Each sale now earns more than it costs. Families who first met your salespeople at home now buy filters in shops and online. Aquaguard remains a name India knows for water purifiers.

text.text: For about 25 years, your salespeople built a name Indian families trusted for clean water. Then rivals grew by selling in shops. Years later, your company is sold. Its new owners sell in shops and online too. By 2025, only about a quarter of sales happen at the door.
Your large sales team keeps your brand alive, but each sale costs more every year. Rivals sell machines in shops, and your lead slowly gets smaller.
You change how you sell in the end, but earlier mistakes cost you years. Your brand survives, while rivals selling in shops keep much of the lead you could have had.
Many families know your brand, but some sales cost more than they earn. Rivals selling in shops catch up, and your lead slowly gets smaller.
Families once trusted your name, but your costs grew faster than sales. Rivals selling in shops won many customers, and your company became a small player.
You changed how you sold, but too late. Families never came to trust your name. Rivals won the buyers you tried to reach, and your company became a small player.
Families never come to trust your name. Rivals selling in shops win the buyers you tried to reach, and your company becomes a small player.

fired.title: The owners lose faith
fired.text: After three costly decisions, the owners no longer trust you to run the company. They appoint a new chief.

realHistory: Eureka Forbes began in 1982 as a joint company of the Tata group's Forbes & Company and Sweden's Electrolux. It sold its Euroclean vacuum cleaners in homes, not shops, and in the 1980s added Aquaguard, India's first water purifier. From one Bombay office with 20 salespeople in 1987, its door-to-door team grew to more than 8,000 by 2014. It talked many families out of boiling water, and Aquaguard held three in four purifier sales in 2004–05. A company plumber fitted each machine, technicians came back to service it, and service became a big, steady income. Then rivals came in, and gated buildings made knocking on doors harder: its share fell to about six in ten by 2012. Under new owners since 2022, it sells through shops and online too; by 2025 direct sales were about a quarter of the total.
